21|BACKGROUND
22|The cardiovascular effects of adding once-weekly treatment with exenatide to usual
23|care in patients with type 2 diabetes are unknown.
24|METHODS
25|We randomly assigned patients with type 2 diabetes, with or without previous car-
26|diovascular disease, to receive subcutaneous injections of extended-release exenatide
27|at a dose of 2 mg or matching placebo once weekly. The primary composite out-
28|come was the first occurrence of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myo-
29|cardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. The coprimary hypotheses were that exena-
30|tide, administered once weekly, would be noninferior to placebo with respect to
31|safety and superior to placebo with respect to efficacy.
32|RESULTS
33|In all, 14,752 patients (of whom 10,782 [73.1%] had previous cardiovascular
34|disease) were followed for a median of 3.2 years (interquartile range, 2.2 to 4.4).
35|A primary composite outcome event occurred in 839 of 7356 patients (11.4%; 3.7
36|events per 100 person-years) in the exenatide group and in 905 of 7396 patients
37|(12.2%; 4.0 events per 100 person-years) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.91;
38|95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.00), with the intention-to-treat analysis
39|indicating that exenatide, administered once weekly, was noninferior to placebo with
40|respect to safety (P<0.001 for noninferiority) but was not superior to placebo
41|with respect to efficacy (P = 0.06 for superiority). The rates of death from cardio-
42|vascular causes, fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke,
43|hospitalization for heart failure, and hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome,
44|and the incidence of acute pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, medullary thyroid
45|carcinoma, and serious adverse events did not differ significantly between the two
46|groups.
47|CONCLUSIONS
48|Among patients with type 2 diabetes with or without previous cardiovascular
49|disease, the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events did not differ sig-
50|nificantly between patients who received exenatide and those who received pla-
51|cebo. (Funded by Amylin Pharmaceuticals; EXSCEL ClinicalTrials.gov number,
52|NCT01144338.)

4|T
5|he risk of death from any cause
6|among persons with type 2 diabetes is up
7|to twice that of the general population,1
8|and the risk of death from cardiovascular causes
9|is up to four times that of the general popula-
10|tion.2,3 Improved glycemic control has been shown
11|to improve microvascular outcomes,4,5 but a bene-
12|ficial effect on macrovascular outcomes is less
13|certain.6 In trials that assessed cardiovascular
14|outcomes associated with the use of newer glucose-
15|lowering agents, no effect on major adverse
16|cardiovascular events (MACE) was shown with
17|three dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitors
18|(saxagliptin, alogliptin, and sitagliptin)7-9 and one
19|exendin-4-based glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)
20|receptor agonist (lixisenatide),10 but a lower risk
21|of MACE was shown with two GLP-1 receptor
22|agonists (liraglutide and semaglutide)11,12 and
23|two sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2)
24|inhibitors (empagliflozin and canagliflozin).13,14
25|A once-weekly, injectable, extended-release for-
26|mulation of exenatide, an exendin-4-based GLP-1
27|receptor agonist approved for the treatment of
28|type 2 diabetes, has been shown to lower blood
29|glucose and induce modest decreases in body
30|weight, blood pressure, and lipid levels15,16 but
31|has also been shown to increase heart rate.17,18
32|In accordance with regulatory guidance,19,20 the
33|Exenatide Study of Cardiovascular Event Lower-
34|ing (EXSCEL) assessed the long-term cardiovas-
35|cular safety and efficacy of exenatide, administered
36|once weekly, in patients with type 2 diabetes
37|who had a wide range of cardiovascular risk.
38|Methods
39|Trial Oversight
40|We conducted this pragmatic, randomized, double-
41|blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial at
42|687 sites in 35 countries. The design of this aca-
43|demically led trial has been reported previously.21
44|A diagram showing the overall design is provided
45|in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, avail-
46|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.
47|The trial was conducted jointly by the Duke
48|Clinical Research Institute and the University of
49|Oxford Diabetes Trials Unit in collaboration with
50|the sponsor, Amylin Pharmaceuticals, a wholly
51|owned subsidiary of AstraZeneca. The protocol,
52|which was approved by the ethics committee at
53|each participating site, and the statistical analy-
54|sis plan are available at NEJM.org. The statistical
55|analyses were performed by the Duke Clinical
56|Research Institute, independent of the sponsor.
57|Details of the trial organization and a complete
58|list of the investigators are provided in the Sup-
59|plementary Appendix.
60|All the patients provided written informed
61|consent. Our trial was designed and overseen by
62|a steering committee composed of nine investi-
63|gators and two employees of the sponsor. An
64|independent data and safety monitoring commit-
65|tee, who had access to unblinded data, performed
66|regular safety surveillance. All the authors had
67|access to the final trial results and vouch for the
68|accuracy and completeness of the data and
69|analyses and for the fidelity of the trial to the
70|protocol. The manuscript, drafted by the second
71|and third authors, was revised and approved by
72|all the authors, who assume responsibility for its
73|accuracy and completeness and made the deci-
74|sion to submit the manuscript for publication.
75|Trial Population
76|Adults with type 2 diabetes (defined as a glycated
77|hemoglobin level of 6.5 to 10.0% [48 to 96 mmol
78|per mole]) were eligible for participation in the
79|trial. The trial was designed such that approxi-
80|mately 70% of enrolled patients would have had
81|previous cardiovascular events and 30% would
82|not have had previous cardiovascular events.
83|Previous cardiovascular events were defined as a
84|history of major clinical manifestation of coro-
85|nary artery disease, ischemic cerebrovascular dis-
86|ease, or atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease.
87|Patients were permitted to receive up to three
88|oral glucose-lowering agents or to receive insulin,
89|either alone or in combination with up to two
90|oral glucose-lowering agents. Key exclusion cri-
91|teria were a history of two or more episodes of
92|severe hypoglycemia (defined as hypoglycemia for
93|which a patient received third-party assistance)
94|during the preceding 12 months, end-stage kid-
95|ney disease or an estimated glomerular filtra-
96|tion rate (eGFR) at entry of less than 30 ml per
97|minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, a per-
98|sonal or family history of medullary thyroid car-
99|cinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2,
100|a baseline calcitonin level of greater than 40 ng
101|per liter, or previous treatment with a GLP-1
102|receptor agonist.
103|Randomization and Trial Regimen
104|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
105|to receive subcutaneous injections of extended-
106|release exenatide at a dose of 2 mg or matching

5|system assigned patients on the basis of computer-
6|generated block randomization within each site,
7|with stratification according to history of car-
8|diovascular disease. Patients were required to
9|discontinue the trial regimen if they had two or
10|more occurrences of severe hypoglycemia be-
11|tween trial visits (despite adjustment of other
12|glucose-lowering agents), if they had irreversible
13|kidney dysfunction (confirmed by two consecu-
14|tive eGFR values of <30 ml per minute per 1.73 m2)
15|or received renal-replacement therapy, or if they
16|were found to have an elevated calcitonin level
17|(>40 ng per liter at baseline or ≥50 ng per liter
18|thereafter). Calcitonin levels were measured at a
19|central laboratory at baseline and annually there-
20|after. Other laboratory values were obtained from
21|usual-care blood sampling, which was consistent
22|with the pragmatic design of the trial. In order to
23|minimize potential confounding effects of dif-
24|ferential glycemic levels on trial outcomes, the
25|use of open-label glucose-lowering agents (includ-
26|ing DPP-4 inhibitors but not including GLP-1
27|receptor agonists) was encouraged to promote
28|glycemic equipoise between the two trial groups
29|and to help patients reach clinically appropriate
30|glycated hemoglobin targets.
31|Outcomes
32|The primary outcome was defined as the first
33|occurrence of any component of the composite
34|outcome of death from cardiovascular causes,
35|nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke
36|(three-component MACE outcome), in a time-to-
37|event analysis. Secondary outcomes included
38|death from any cause, death from cardiovascular
39|causes, and the first occurrence of nonfatal or
40|fatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal or fatal
41|stroke, hospitalization for acute coronary syn-
42|drome, and hospitalization for heart failure, in
43|time-to-event analyses. An independent clinical
44|events classification committee whose members
45|were unaware of the trial-group assignments ad-
46|judicated all the components of the primary com-
47|posite outcome, secondary outcomes, ventricular
48|arrhythmias that led to intervention, neoplasms,
49|and pancreatitis; these events are defined in the
50|Clinical Event Definitions section in the Supple-
51|mentary Appendix.
52|Additional outcomes that were prespecified
53|in the protocol included a composite of death
54|from cardiovascular causes or hospitalization for
55|heart failure, the first confirmed revasculariza-
56|tion procedure, initiation of the first interven-
57|tional glucose-lowering medication received dur-
58|ing the trial other than the trial regimen, and
59|absolute values and changes from baseline in
60|glycated hemoglobin level, body weight, blood
61|pressure, and lipid levels. Prespecified events of
62|clinical interest for which information was col-
63|lected systematically at every follow-up visit,
64|regardless of seriousness, were pancreatitis, neo-
65|plasm, severe hypoglycemia, and expected car-
66|diovascular or diabetes-related complications.
67|Information on other nonserious adverse events
68|was not collected (details are provided in Section
69|10.3 in the protocol).
70|Patients were followed for adverse events un-
71|til the end of the trial or 70 days after discon-
72|tinuation of the trial regimen. For patients who
73|were either lost to follow-up or had withdrawn
74|consent, vital status was ascertained during the
75|70-day washout period by searches conducted
76|with the use of local or national electronic
77|health records, death registries, or other publicly
78|available sources (as permitted by local ethics
79|approvals).
80|Statistical Analysis
81|Information on sample size and power calcula-
82|tions has been published previously 21; we esti-
83|mated that with 1360 patients with a confirmed
84|primary composite outcome event, the trial would
85|have 85% power to detect a risk of a primary
86|composite outcome event that was 15% lower
87|with once-weekly administration of exenatide
88|than with placebo, at a two-sided alpha level of
89|0.05. The time-to-event analyses were performed
90|with the use of a Cox proportional-hazards
91|model for primary, secondary, and exploratory
92|outcomes in the intention-to-treat population,
93|stratified according to history of cardiovascular
94|disease, with trial regimen as an explanatory
95|variable. The intention-to-treat population includ-
96|ed all patients who underwent randomization.
97|The Kaplan-Meier method was used to calculate
98|event rates. The primary safety hypothesis was
99|that exenatide, administered once weekly, would
100|be noninferior to placebo for the primary out-
101|come, with a noninferiority margin of 1.3 for the
102|upper limit of the two-sided 95% confidence
103|interval of the hazard ratio. The primary efficacy
104|hypothesis was that exenatide, administered once
105|weekly, would be superior to placebo, with a

9|come, superiority for the primary composite
10|outcome, superiority for all-cause mortality, supe-

16|for heart failure (tested with the use of the Hoch

18|cal testing plan, if a significant difference was
19|not found for an outcome, formal hypothesis
20|testing was not to be conducted for the remain-
21|ing ordered outcomes.
22|Sensitivity analyses of the primary efficacy
23|outcome were performed in the per-protocol
24|population, which included all randomized pa-
25|tients who received at least one dose of the trial
26|regimen and had no major protocol violations
27|(see the protocol for further details). The safety
28|analyses were performed in patients who under-
29|went randomization and received at least one
30|dose of exenatide or placebo.
31|Baseline characteristics were summarized as
32|means and standard deviations, medians and
33|interquartile ranges, or percentages. The primary
34|composite outcome was analyzed in prespecified
35|subgroups that were defined according to base-
36|line characteristics, including age at randomiza-
37|tion, sex, race, geographic region, type of glucose-
38|lowering therapy, duration of diabetes, history
39|or no history of a cardiovascular event or heart
40|failure, body-mass index, glycated hemoglobin
41|level, and kidney function. Repeated measures,
42|such as glycated hemoglobin level and body
43|weight, were analyzed with the use of longitudi-
44|nal models with mixed effects, with differences
45|between the trial groups estimated by least-
46|squares mean differences with 95% confidence
47|intervals. Analyses were conducted with the use
48|of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
49|Results
50|Trial Patients
51|In all, 14,752 patients (of whom 10,782 [73.1%]
52|had previous cardiovascular disease) underwent
53|randomization from June 18, 2010, through Sep-
54|tember 16, 2015, and were included in the inten-
55|tion-to-treat population; 7356 patients were as-
56|signed to receive exenatide and 7396 to receive
57|placebo once weekly (Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
58|tary Appendix).22 The planned closeout of follow-
59|up of the patients was from December 5, 2016,
60|to May 11, 2017, after the prespecified required
61|minimum of 1360 patients were confirmed to
62|have had a primary composite outcome event.
63|The demographic, disease, and clinical char-
64|acteristics of the patients did not differ signifi-
65|cantly between the groups, nor did the use of
66|glucose-lowering agents or medications to reduce
67|the risk of cardiovascular disease, with the excep-
68|tion of lipid-lowering medications and SGLT-2
69|inhibitors (Table S1 in the Supplementary Ap-
70|pendix).22 At baseline, the median length of time
71|that patients had had diabetes was 12.0 years
72|(interquartile range, 7.0 to 18.0), the median
73|glycated hemoglobin level was 8.0% (interquar-
74|tile range, 7.3 to 8.9) (63.9 mmol per mole [inter-
75|quartile range, 56.3 to 73.8]), and 2389 patients
76|(16.2%) had a history of heart failure.
77|A total of 14,187 patients (96.2%) completed
78|the trial, and vital status was obtained for 98.8%
79|of the patients. The median duration of follow-
80|up was 3.2 years (interquartile range, 2.2 to 4.4;
81|maximum, 6.8) and was similar in the two
82|groups. The median duration of exposure to the
83|trial regimen was 2.4 years (interquartile range,
84|1.4 to 3.8) in the exenatide group and 2.3 years
85|(interquartile range, 1.2 to 3.6) in the placebo
86|group. The mean percentage of time that partici-
87|pants received the trial regimen (i.e., the dura-
88|tion of time that participants received the trial
89|regimen relative to the duration of time that they
90|were expected to receive the regimen during the
91|trial) was 76.0% and 75.0%, respectively. Prema-
92|ture discontinuation of the trial regimen was
93|primarily the result of decision by the patient
94|(Table S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
